01.actor: A man who spoke offhandedly, whose story Rabbi Hiyya relates
01.event: In passing, a man recalled being carried on his father's shoulder, taken out of school, stripped and immersed so he could eat teruma that evening, and that his friends kept away from him and called him 'Yohanan who eats hallot'.
01.turn: His offhand remark, made without any intent to prove anything, revealed that he had been raised as a priest.
01.outcome: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi elevated him to the priesthood on the strength of his statement.
01.summary: A man was chatting about something else and let slip that as a child he had been taken out of school and immersed so he could eat teruma, and that his friends had shunned him and called him 'Yohanan who eats hallot'. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi accepted this offhand remark and elevated him to the priesthood.

02.event: A man betrothed a woman with a blue marble stone and Rav Hisda sat estimating whether it was worth a peruta; when it was not, he ruled she was not betrothed.
02.turn: The man's mother objected that the stone had been worth a peruta on the day of the betrothal.
02.outcome: Rav Hisda replied it was not in her power to bar the woman to a later suitor; the Sages then pressed him about witnesses and he dismissed them as absent.
02.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a blue marble stone, and Rav Hisda sat and appraised whether it was worth a peruta. The man's mother protested that it had been worth that much on the day of betrothal, but Rav Hisda answered that she could not forbid the woman to a later man. When the Sages noted that witnesses knew it had once been worth a peruta, he said they were not present now.
02.missing: The passage is mainly a ruling attached to brief cases; the bundle-of-rags case has no clear event, and nothing says what became of the woman or the stone.

03.actor: A man drinking wine in a shop and a woman who came in
03.event: A woman asked a man drinking wine in a shop for a cup, and he asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he gave it; she answered 'give to drink, give me to drink'.
03.turn: Her repeated, emphatic reply read as mockery or as not agreeing to his condition rather than as consent.
03.outcome: Rav Hama ruled that such a phrase means nothing and she is not betrothed.
03.summary: A man was drinking wine in a shop when a woman came and asked him for a cup. He asked if she would be betrothed to him if he gave it, and she answered only 'give me to drink, give me to drink'. Rav Hama ruled that this phrase carries no commitment, so she was not betrothed.

04.missing: Rav Aha asks Rav Ashi's students whether he said anything about the doorway form and they say he said nothing; this is a report of an absence of a statement, with no event, turn or outcome.

05.actor: Ravina and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
05.event: Ravina came upon Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak leaning on a door bar, deep in thought over what the law is if a husband says of a bill of divorce only 'void'.
05.summary: Ravina found Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak leaning on the bar of a door, lost in thought over whether a husband who says only 'void' about a bill of divorce has actually voided it. No answer is given and the question stands.
05.missing: No turn and no resolution; it is a scene that merely frames an open legal question.

06.actor: A woman obligated to take an oath in Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court
06.event: The opposing litigant asked that she take the oath in her town, hoping shame would make her admit; she asked for a document of rights to be written for her first, and Rav Beivai ordered it written.
06.turn: Rav Pappi objected, insulting Rav Beivai's family line, because writing the document before the oath looks like falsehood.
06.outcome: Rav Beivai's order stands against Rav Pappi's objection, which is then explained by a statement of Rava.
06.summary: A woman was ordered to swear an oath in Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court, and her opponent asked that she swear in her town where shame might make her confess. She demanded that a document of rights be written for her first, and Rav Beivai agreed. Rav Pappi rebuked him sharply for it.
06.missing: How the case finally ended is not stated.

07.missing: Rabbi Elazar asks Rabbi Asi what was said in the study hall and receives a ruling; this is a vehicle for transmitting a halakhic statement, with no narrative event.

08.event: Rav Kahana, who held beer belonging to an orphan, Rav Mesharshiyya bar Hilkai, delayed selling it until the Festival.
08.turn: He reasoned that although it might sour slightly, it would fetch cash at the Festival.
08.summary: Rav Kahana was holding beer that belonged to an orphan, Rav Mesharshiyya bar Hilkai. He chose to keep it until the Festival, saying that even if it spoiled a little it would bring in ready money then.
08.missing: The passage does not say what happened to the beer or whether anyone objected; it is a precedent for the orphan-property rule.

09.event: Ravina visited Mehoza, where his host brought out a slaughtering knife and showed it to him, and Ravina told him to take it to Rava for examination.
09.turn: The host objected that Rava taught a scholar may examine a knife himself; Ravina answered that he was only buying the meat from him, so the principle did not apply.
09.outcome: Ravina held that the host should have the knife examined, since a scholar's self-inspection covers only his own slaughter.
09.summary: Ravina arrived in Mehoza and his host showed him a slaughtering knife. Ravina told him to take it to Rava to inspect. The host pointed out Rava's rule that a scholar may inspect a knife for himself, and Ravina replied that since he was only buying the meat, the rule did not cover him.

10.actor: The daughter-in-law of the house of the son of Elyashiv
10.event: She was bringing the orphan heirs to court to claim her marriage contract, and they said it was demeaning for her to go in house clothes.
10.turn: She went and put on all her clothes and covered herself with them.
10.outcome: They came before Ravina, who ruled that the court appraises what a widow is wearing, so everything she wore was counted against her marriage contract.
10.summary: A widow was taking the orphan heirs to court for her marriage contract. They told her it shamed them for her to appear in plain house clothes, so she dressed in all her clothes. Before Ravina, the court appraised what she was wearing and counted it against her payment.

11.event: Relatives of Rabbi Yohanan had to care for their father's wife, who needed treatment every day, and came to ask him; he told them to fix a lump sum with the doctor.
11.turn: Rabbi Yohanan later said in regret that they had made themselves like legal advisors.
11.outcome: He came to hold that an important person is different and should not help relatives at another's cost.
11.summary: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives had to pay for their father's widow's daily treatment, and asked him what to do. He told them to agree a fixed fee with the doctor so it would be deducted from her marriage contract. Later he regretted it, saying they had made themselves like legal advisors, because an important person should be more careful.

12.event: A woman was bequeathed 400 dinars in Bei Hozai; her husband took 600 of his own to go and bring them back, and on the way took one dinar of hers for a need.
12.turn: He came before Rabbi Ami, who ruled that what he spent he spent and what he ate he ate; the Rabbis objected that he ate principal, not produce.
12.outcome: Rabbi Ami answered that it is then a case of expense without eating, so he swears how much he spent and takes it.
12.summary: A husband travelled to a distant place with 600 dinars of his own to collect the 400 dinars his wife had inherited, and spent one of hers on the way back. Rabbi Ami ruled that each side had spent and eaten what it had. When the Rabbis said he had eaten principal, Rabbi Ami replied that it is then an expense case in which he swears and collects.

13.actor: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda, Marei bar Mar, Rav Huna and Rabba
13.event: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda sent Marei bar Mar to ask Rav Huna whether the law follows Rabbi Elazar on bills of divorce.
13.turn: Rav Huna died before the request reached him.
13.outcome: His son Rabba answered in his stead that the law follows Rabbi Elazar, citing his father in the name of Rava and other teachers in Rav's name.
13.summary: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda sent word to Marei bar Mar to ask Rav Huna about a ruling on bills of divorce. Rav Huna died before the question could reach him. His son Rabba told Marei bar Mar what his father had taught, that the law follows Rabbi Elazar.

14.missing: A bare list of three sages being served by unknowing human partitions, with no individual event, turn or end.

15.actor: Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
15.event: When Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi fell ill, Rabbi Hiyya visited and found him crying, and asked why, since a baraita says dying while crying is a bad sign.
15.turn: Rabbi explained he was weeping not for himself but for the Torah and mitzvot he would no longer be able to fulfill.
15.outcome: It shows Rabbi Hiyya was with Rabbi at his deathbed.
15.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi fell ill and Rabbi Hiyya came and found him weeping. Hiyya asked why, quoting a teaching that dying in tears is a bad sign. Rabbi answered that he was crying for the Torah and mitzvot he would no longer be able to perform.
15.missing: The text does not describe his death directly.

16.actor: Rav Nahman and the judges of Neharde'a and Pumbedita
16.event: Cases came before the courts in Neharde'a and Pumbedita in which daughters were supported from movable property, and the judges ruled and collected accordingly.
16.turn: Rav Nahman ordered them to reverse their decisions.
16.outcome: He threatened to collect their houses from them if they did not.
16.summary: Courts in Neharde'a and Pumbedita ordered orphans' movable property to be used to support daughters. Rav Nahman told the judges to reverse their rulings, or he would seize their houses to compensate those they ruled against.
16.missing: Whether the judges complied is not stated, and the facts of the cases are not given.

17.actor: A woman of Mehoza married to a man of Neharde'a, and Rav Nahman
17.event: She and her husband came before Rav Nahman over her marriage contract, and he heard from her accent that she was from Mehoza.
17.turn: He ruled Babylonia follows Rav, but they objected that she was marrying into Neharde'a.
17.outcome: He accepted this and ruled that Neharde'a and its towns follow Shmuel, extending as far as the Neharde'a kav is used.
17.summary: A woman from Mehoza who had married into Neharde'a came before Rav Nahman about her marriage contract. He recognised her accent and said Babylonia follows Rav. They objected that she lived in Neharde'a, so he ruled that Neharde'a and its towns follow Shmuel.

18.missing: Mareimar's habit of blocking Sura's alleyways with nets and his stated concern is a practice and its reasoning, with no particular event.

19.event: Peleimu used to say daily 'an arrow in the eye of Satan'; on the eve of Yom Kippur Satan came disguised as a pauper, and Peleimu fed him and seated him at the table, where he behaved repulsively.
19.turn: Peleimu told him to sit properly, Satan spat in a cup and pretended to die, and Peleimu was accused of killing a man and fled into the bathroom.
19.outcome: Satan revealed himself and told Peleimu to say instead 'let the Merciful One rebuke Satan'.
19.summary: Peleimu mocked Satan daily. On the eve of Yom Kippur Satan came as a pauper, was fed and seated at the table, behaved repulsively, then spat in a cup and feigned death. Peleimu was accused of killing a man and fled, and Satan revealed himself and told him to say 'may the Merciful One rebuke Satan' instead.

20.event: Rabba ruled on a bill of divorce found in a flax house in Pumbedita, according to his own halakhic reasoning.
20.outcome: Two versions give different details of the place and whether two same-named people were established.
20.summary: Rabba issued a practical ruling about a bill of divorce found in a flax house in Pumbedita. One account says it was where flax was soaked, away from caravans, the other that it was where flax was sold and caravans are common.
20.missing: The ruling itself and what happened to the document are not stated; the passage only reports that he acted, with disputed details.
